title: How do we find the mean from a table of frequencies?
description: A table lists family sizes from three to ten and how many students have each size. Each size is multiplied by its frequency, the amounts are added, and the total is divided by thirty six students. Keeko doubts this and divides the frequencies by the eight sizes.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply each size by its frequency, add the amounts, then divide by the number of students. Watch for students who add the frequencies and divide by the number of sizes.

source: Find the mean family size of the class from the table: size 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 occurs 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1 times.
video_script.why: A child who finds a mean from a short list meets a frequency table for the first time.
video_script.substitution: the book's table of family sizes 3 to 10 with frequencies 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1
video_script.anchor: the table of family sizes with a frequency under each size
video_script.wrong_answer: the mean is four point five
video_script.wrong_move: adds the frequencies to get 36 and divides by the 8 sizes, 36 ÷ 8 = 4.5; the sizes themselves never enter
video_script.payoff_line: The mean family size is about five point two two

final_answer.spoken: the mean family size is about five point two two

names.Laksh: class teacher who collects the family sizes of the class

never_show: 4.5 as the mean, marked as right
maths_rules: slip: 36 ÷ 8 = 4.5 divides the number of students by the number of sizes, which means nothing
video_script.design: One table all video. Each size is multiplied by its frequency, the amounts are added, and the total is divided by the number of students. Keeko's wrong idea is to divide the frequencies by the number of sizes.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; Laksh at the board; a table with family sizes 3 to 10 in the top row and student counts 3, 11, 9, 7, 3, 1, 1, 1 in the bottom row

marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.ask: the words mean family size appear with an empty box

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean.
<bookmark mark='story'/>Laksh asks every student how many people live in the family.
<bookmark mark='table'/>The answers go into a table. The top row shows family sizes from three to ten. The bottom row shows how many students have each size.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the mean family size of the class?

beats.on_screen: the table and the question stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the bottom row labelled frequency; size 3 has frequency 3, size 4 has frequency 11

marks.freq: the bottom row is labelled frequency
marks.big: size 4 is shown 11 times in a row of small dots, size 3 only 3 times

narration: <bookmark mark='freq'/>The number of students with each family size is called the frequency.
<bookmark mark='big'/>A size with a big frequency occurs many times in the data. Size four occurs eleven times, and size three only three times.

marks.given: the sizes and their frequencies are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, family sizes three to ten. Their frequencies are three, eleven, nine, seven, three, one, one and one.

beats.on_screen: To find: the mean family size

marks.find: the words the mean family size are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the mean family size of the class.

marks.add: the eight frequencies are added one by one

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step one, add the frequencies to count the students. Three plus eleven plus nine plus seven plus three plus one plus one plus one.
<bookmark mark='total'/>That gives thirty six students.

marks.p3: 7 × 3 = 21 is written, then 8, 9 and 10 each written with × 1

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, multiply each family size by its frequency.
<bookmark mark='p1'/>Three times three is nine. Four times eleven is forty four.
<bookmark mark='p2'/>Five times nine is forty five. Six times seven is forty two.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>Seven times three is twenty one. Sizes eight, nine and ten occur once each, so they give eight, nine and ten.

marks.add: the eight amounts line up in a row
marks.rest: 21, 8, 9 and 10 are added on to reach 188

narration: <bookmark mark='add'/>Step three, add the amounts to get the total of all the family members.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Nine plus forty four plus forty five plus forty two is one hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>Adding twenty one, eight, nine and ten gives one hundred and eighty eight.

marks.rule: the line mean = total ÷ students appears

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step four, the mean is the total divided by the number of students.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Divide one hundred and eighty eight by thirty six.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The mean family size is about five point two two.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the table
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: the frequencies add to 36, and 36 ÷ 8 sizes = 4.5; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: Keeko's bubble shows the mean as 4.5
marks.why: the sizes row is greyed out inside the bubble
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and size × frequency is lit up

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the mean is four point five.
<bookmark mark='move'/>Keeko added the frequencies to get thirty six and divided by the eight sizes.
<bookmark mark='why'/>But thirty six counts students, not family members. The sizes themselves never entered the sum.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>A size shared by many students must count for more. That is why each size is multiplied by its frequency.
